event.t: Brent settled at $92.44 a barrel on Monday 16 November, down $3.40, or about 3.5%. US crude (WTI) settled at $85.72, down $2.84, or 3.2%.
Reuters says recovering oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz strengthened expectations of a supply surplus. New tanker incidents showed that Middle East exports are still at risk.
The International Energy Agency said on Friday that it expects supply to be 1.7 million barrels a day above demand in the fourth quarter. It had earlier forecast a shortage.
On Friday 13 November Brent had settled at $95.84, after two weekly falls in a row.
Prices can still jump on war news: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Sunday that they attacked a US base in Bahrain.

summary: Brent crude settled at $92.44 a barrel on Monday 16 November, down $3.40 or about 3.5%. Traders expect more supply than demand as oil exports from the Middle East recover.

updates.t: Brent slips to $95.37 early on Monday (01:45 GMT) as traders expect a supply surplus. It settled at $95.84 on Friday, its second weekly fall in a row.
Brent settles at $92.44 on Monday, down $3.40 or about 3.5%, as recovering Middle East exports strengthen expectations of a supply surplus. US crude settles at $85.72.

Brent is steady on Tuesday at $92.61 at 09:10 GMT, up 17 cents, after dipping to $91.66 earlier in Asia. Reuters says the expected surplus balances worries about tanker attacks. Brent has fallen 22% so far this month.
Brent settled near $93 a barrel on Tuesday after swinging in a range of about $3, as attacks around the Strait of Hormuz offset forecasts of a supply surplus.
Brent fell below $92 a barrel on Wednesday morning, as recovering supplies and higher US stockpiles outweighed new fighting in the Gulf, Bloomberg reports.

why: Oil feeds into fuel, transport, food and heating costs. Lower prices ease inflation, which matters for what central banks do next. But the market is pulled two ways: more supply on one side, and a war that can disrupt it at any time on the other.
